subject: Chemistry
title: Nitrogen Triiodide: Touch and Boom
description: A 60-second lesson on Nitrogen Triiodide: Touch and Boom.

hook.text: Nitrogen triiodide is so sensitive that a feather's touch sets it off with a purple flash and a bang.

buildup.text: It's made by mixing iodine crystals with ammonia. When wet, it's harmless. When dry, it's terrifying.

discovery.text: The nitrogen-iodine bonds are extremely strained. Any vibration breaks them, releasing energy instantly.

twist.text: Chemistry teachers love it for demonstrations. Paint it on a surface, let it dry, and watch students jump.

climax.text: The purple cloud is iodine vapor. The loud crack comes from gas expanding faster than sound.

punchline.text: A feather sets it off. Purple smoke and a bang. Chemistry's best demo.

quiz.question: Why is nitrogen triiodide so sensitive to touch?
options: Its chemical bonds are extremely strained and break from any vibration
It absorbs moisture from skin and reacts
It contains radioactive isotopes that decay on contact

details.summary: Nitrogen triiodide is an extremely sensitive contact explosive that detonates from the slightest touch, a feather's brush, or even a puff of air. When dry, the compound's nitrogen-iodine bonds break with minimal energy input, releasing violet iodine vapor and a sharp crack.
details.whyItMatters: Nitrogen triiodide is a dramatic classroom demonstration of activation energy and bond instability. Its extreme sensitivity illustrates why certain chemical structures are inherently unstable.
takeaways: NI3 detonates from the lightest physical contact when dry
The explosion produces a purple cloud of iodine vapor
It is safe to prepare wet but becomes dangerous as it dries

faq.question: Why is nitrogen triiodide so much more sensitive than other explosives?
faq.answer: The three large iodine atoms crowd around the small nitrogen atom, creating enormous molecular strain. The nitrogen-iodine bonds are weak and the product nitrogen gas is extremely stable, so minimal energy tips the balance toward explosive decomposition.

faq.question: Is nitrogen triiodide used in any practical applications?
faq.answer: No. It has no practical applications because it cannot be stored, transported, or controlled safely. Its only use is as a chemistry demonstration to illustrate concepts of activation energy, molecular instability, and the relationship between structure and reactivity.
